title: The White House Just Launched Its First Major H-1B Fraud Investigation. Seventy-Three Per Cent of Visa Holders Are Indian.
excerpt: Vice President Vance and the Labor Department's inspector general have fired dozens of subpoenas targeting healthcare fraud, wage kickbacks, and what they call a system 'tied to cartels.' For hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals in America, the scrutiny just got personal.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • The White House launched a major investigation into H-1B visa fraud targeting healthcare and wage issues.
  • 73% of H-1B visa holders are Indian, with many working in tech and healthcare sectors.
  • The probe links visa fraud to organized crime and violent crime, according to the Labor Department.
  • H-1B approvals for Indian IT firms have dropped nearly 40% this year amid tightening visa rules.
  • Political rhetoric risks conflating fraudulent actors with legitimate visa holders, raising concerns for Indian professionals.

The Trump administration's crackdown on immigration fraud has entered a new phase. On Wednesday, Vice President JD Vance and Labor Department Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito announced the government's first major investigation into H-1B and PERM visa fraud, firing dozens of subpoenas in what they describe as a sweeping probe into healthcare fraud, forced-labor networks, and wage suppression. The investigation, announced at an anti-fraud event in Milwaukee, targets what the DOL's Office of Inspector General says are "widespread schemes in which employers and labor brokers submitted fraudulent applications, exploited foreign workers through coercive wage-kickback arrangements, and undercut American workers by flooding the market with below-wage labor." ## The Scale of the Problem The numbers are stark. Department of Homeland Security assessments have found that as much as 21 per cent of H-1B petitions are fraudulent. According to Pew Research, 73 per cent of all H-1B workers come from India, more than half hold master's degrees, and the majority work in programming, data communications, or technical support roles at companies like Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, and Apple. D'Esposito told Fox Business that the probe extends beyond H-1B holders to employment-based green card recipients. He linked the fraud to organised crime: "This is another example where fraud is fueling violent crime. Much of the visa and human trafficking that we see when it comes to this foreign labor is tied to cartels, tied to transnational gangs." > **"He linked the fraud to organised crime: "This is another example where fraud is fueling violent crime."** The inspector general singled out the healthcare sector, claiming that fraudulent visa holders have been used to "bilk the medical industry to the tune of hundreds of millions of dollars" and that "these are people working in medical facilities and doctors' offices that are actually putting people in harm's way." ## What Vance Said Vance framed the probe as a defence of the visa programme's original purpose. "This is a visa program that was set up to ensure that if you were a brilliant technology person or a brilliant scientist or a brilliant doctor, you could come to the United States," he told attendees. "But what's happening way too much is that big corporations and fraudsters overseas are using this program to undercut the wages of American workers." His message was blunt: "If you are trying to take advantage of that visa program, you are not allowed in to the United States of America." ## The Context for Indian Professionals
Impact on Indian Professionals
›Tightening visa rules affect Indian IT firms significantly.
›Political rhetoric may harm legitimate visa holders.
›Healthcare sector under scrutiny for fraudulent practices.
›Visa program originally aimed at skilled professionals.
The probe arrives against a backdrop of escalating restrictions that have reshaped the landscape for Indian workers in America. President Trump signed an executive order last year imposing a $100,000 annual fee on all H-1B applicants — though a federal judge struck that down in June. The Department of Housing and Urban Development stopped non-permanent residents, including H-1B holders, from qualifying for FHA-insured mortgages in May 2025. And the administration's social media vetting requirements at consulates have caused months-long delays for Indians returning from visa stamping trips home. The timing is particularly sensitive. H-1B approvals for India's top IT firms — TCS, Infosys, Wipro — have slumped nearly 40 per cent this year as the administration tightens visa rules. Meanwhile, the broader crackdown on Day 1 CPT programmes threatens thousands of Indian professionals who used those pathways to maintain legal status. California, New York, Illinois, Texas, and Washington State receive the most H-1B petitions. H-1B recipients peaked at 442,425 approvals in 2022 under President Biden. ## Why the Diaspora Should Watch Closely For the vast majority of Indian H-1B holders — skilled engineers, data scientists, doctors, and researchers who entered the system legally and work at legitimate companies — the probe creates an uncomfortable paradox. The fraud it targets is real, and it undermines the credibility of a programme that hundreds of thousands of Indian families depend on. But the political rhetoric surrounding the investigation rarely distinguishes between fraudulent actors and the qualified majority. The investigation's scope — covering healthcare, technology, and manufacturing sectors — means its effects will ripple across the industries where Indian professionals are most concentrated. Whether it results in meaningful reforms that protect both American workers and legitimate visa holders, or becomes another lever for broader restrictions, will depend on how narrowly the subpoenas are targeted and how the findings are used. Trump himself has sent mixed signals. Before returning to the White House, he told the New York Post that he had "always been in favour of the visas" and had used H-1Bs to hire workers for his own properties. The gap between that statement and his administration's enforcement posture is where the uncertainty lives — and where the diaspora's anxiety is most acute.
